# Deep Level Haulage: Control Room Platform

## The situation

An underground mine runs a fleet of twelve autonomous battery-electric haul trucks. They carry rock (ore) from deep in the mine up to a dumping point, around a single one-way loop of tunnel about 1.6 km long. On each lap, a truck:
1. Starts at the **bay**, where trucks park and recharge.
2. Drives down a sloping tunnel (the **decline**) to the lower level.
3. Follows the level's tunnels (**L4 North**) to the **draw point**, where it is loaded with ore.
4. Carries the load along **L4 South** and up a second sloping tunnel (the **incline**).
5. Empties the load at the **tip**, then returns to the bay and starts the next lap.

Each of these stretches is a named zone in `PROTOCOL.md` §3.

The trucks operate themselves. People in a control room on the surface supervise them. These operators need to see what every truck is doing, step in when something is wrong, and sometimes drive a truck by hand from their desk. When a truck breaks down in a tunnel, the operator has to drive it back to the bay.

Several times a shift, the blasting crew closes a section of tunnel for a blast, with about two minutes' notice. **No truck may be inside a closed section.** (The blasting crew keeps people out of the area; that's not your concern here.) The trucks don't know about blasts, so keeping them out falls to the control room.

Two things make this harder than it sounds:
- **The radio network is unreliable.** Messages from the trucks can arrive late, out of order, twice or not at all, and the whole connection to the site sometimes drops.
- **The trucks' data isn't always right.** Some of what they report will be wrong, inconsistent or incomplete. Part of the job is noticing when, and deciding what to do about it.

You are building the control room's software: the first version the operators will actually use.

### Priya: control room operator, day shift, 6 years

> "When the shot firer calls, I have to answer 'is L4 South clear?' within about ten seconds. On the old system I count dots on a map, and I've miscounted."

> "The radio will tell you it got the command, and then the truck just… doesn't. So you send it again. And again. Then you're not sure how many you've sent."

> "If a truck's data is old, show me where it *last* was and how long ago. I can work with that. A blank is useless."

> "We had a near miss last year. My colleague took a truck to drive it out of the draw point, and I didn't know. I sent it a command and couldn't work out why it wasn't listening."

> "Honestly, if the data's stale I'd rather see nothing than see something wrong. Wrong is what gets people hurt."

automation wanted here is deterministic and rule-based. No LLM on the control path in v1. An LLM may sit *beside* it: an operator can ask questions in plain language (answered from the fleet state and logs), or
phrase a command, which the model turns into a **proposal** — never an action.
The operator confirms it, and it then passes through exactly the same
deterministic checks as a button press. Beyond the MVP floor; build only if
time allows.

Sends no commands.\nimport json, os, re, socket, ssl, sys, time\n\ndef env_from(path):\n    vals = {}\n    for line in open(path):\n        m = re.match(r'\\s*(GATEWAY_[A-Z]+)=(.*)\\s*$', line)\n        if m: vals[m.group(1)] = m.group(2).strip()\n    return vals\n\ncfg = env_from(sys.argv[1]); out = open(sys.argv[2], 'w'); duration = float(sys.argv[3])\nhost, port, email = cfg['GATEWAY_HOST'], int(cfg['GATEWAY_PORT']), cfg['GATEWAY_EMAIL']\ndef log(kind, **kw):\n    kw.update(kind=kind, rx_ms=int(time.time()*1000))\n    out.write(json.dumps(kw).replace(email, '<email>') + '\\n'); out.flush()\n\nend = time.time() + duration; attempt = 0\nctx = ssl.create_default_context()\nwhile time.time() < end:\n    attempt += 1\n    try:\n        raw = socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=10)\n        s = ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=host); s.settimeout(5)\n        log('connected', attempt=attempt)\n        s.sendall((json.dumps({'type': 'auth', 'email': email}) + '\\n').encode())\n        buf = b''\n        while time.time() < end:\n            try: chunk = s.recv(65536)\n            except socket.timeout: log('rx_timeout'); continue\n            if not chunk: log('closed_by_peer'); break\n            buf += chunk\n            while b'\\n' in buf:\n                line, buf = buf.split(b'\\n', 1)\n                try: log('msg', m=json.loads(line))\n                except Exception: log('unparseable', raw=line.decode('utf-8', 'replace')[:500])\n        s.close()\n    except Exception as e:\n        log('error', err=repr(e))\n    if time.time() < end: time.sleep(min(2 ** min(attempt, 4), 10))\nlog('done')\nEOF\ncd /Volumes/Transcend/control_room && grep -q '^GATEWAY_EMAIL=.\\+@' .env && echo \"email present\" && python3 --version",
 "description": "Write passive capture script to scratchpad"
}

### Agent (2026-10-02T01:09:39.534Z)

I've committed the `.gitignore` and watched the live gateway for 6 minutes. I haven't written PLAN.md yet. You asked to disagree with me before we commit to a plan, and the brief says the plan stays as written once it exists. So below are the findings, the risk, and the assumptions I'd change; I'll write the plan after you've pushed back.

## Housekeeping

- **`.gitignore` is committed alone** (`982cbe0`). I left out the trailing ```` ``` ```` from CONTEXT.md's code block; copied literally it would have stopped `*.zip` from being ignored. I checked that `.env`, the zip and every `._*` file are ignored.
- **`.env` is a shell script, not a dotenv file.** It contains the `cd …; cat > .env <<'EOF'` command that was meant to create it. Sourcing it would overwrite it, and `docker compose` won't parse it. I didn't change it; it needs fixing before anything reads it.
- **The capture is about 20,800 messages** in `scratchpad/capture.jsonl`, with the email replaced by a placeholder. It sent only `auth` and no commands.

## What the live site does, compared with PROTOCOL.md

The six-minute capture included two blast windows (one full DECLINE cycle and an L4_SOUTH closure starting) and no link drop. Heartbeats arrived every 2.0 s without fail.

**Things the spec doesn't mention, and which would mislead a straightforward client:**

1. **Telemetry can arrive on time and still be wrong.** HT-09 reported `TRAMMING` at 3.0 m/s with its seq counting up, while its position stayed at exactly 306.0 m in DECLINE for over 3 minutes. That covers the whole blast window and continued after it ended. Every freshness check passes, and only comparing reported speed with actual movement catches it. Dave's "wrong is what gets people hurt" is about exactly this case.
2. **Sequence counters reset.** HT-10's counter dropped from 537 back to 1 partway through the capture, while its device clock carried on normally. A client that drops anything with seq ≤ the last one seen would have shown HT-10 stuck at the draw point for about 108 s while it was actually driving.
3. **HT-05 reports `soc_pct` as a fraction** (0.61 instead of 61), every message, the whole time.
4. **HT-08 sends malformed fields** in about 2% of messages: null `speed_mps`, null or missing `soc_pct`, `offset_m` as a string, and `"tramming"` in lowercase.
5. **About 0.2% of lines are cut off part-way but still end in a newline,** so each arrives as an incomplete JSON object.
6. **One truck can go silent while the link looks healthy.** HT-03 dropped out three times, for 26–35 s each, while heartbeats kept arriving.
7. **Clock skew is large.** HT-11's clock is 58 minutes ahead and HT-09's is 3 s behind. Out-of-order telemetry arrives up to about 0.9 s late.

**Things the spec says, which the data showed to matter more than it sounds:**

8. **The battery gauge is a trap.** HT-06 drained from 40% to 9.9% in 6 minutes, against about 1% a minute for the rest of the fleet. It entered the incline loaded at 9.9%. The trucks only go to charge if they're below 25% when they reach the bay, and HT-06 passed the bay above that. I expect it to die in the incline, which is Sam's four-hour recovery. Its drain rate had already marked it as weak within the first 60 s.
9. **A truck can't drive through DECLINE inside the warning time.** Every closure gave exactly 120 s of notice. DECLINE takes about 167 s to cross at 3 m/s. So enforcing a closure has two parts: getting trucks out, and **holding trucks before they enter**. Holding has to happen early enough to cover up to 6 s of command delay, which is about 18 m of travel.
10. **The sim doesn't keep trucks apart.** Pairs drove within 5 m of each other for up to 29 s, and trucks loading at the draw point report the same position. Your open question 3 about headway is showing up in the data, and `EXIT_ZONE` in reverse could back into another truck.
11. **Blasts are frequent.** There were two windows in 6 minutes, and a DECLINE closure lasted about 100 s. Their 15-minute unattended run will probably include 3–5 closures.
12. **HT-07 faulted with `HYD_PRESSURE_LOW` in the incline**, with no prompting. That's the remote-driving case: the truck can only be moved by hand at reduced speed.

**One for you to know:** because nothing was enforcing the rule, HT-04 drove through DECLINE while it was `CLOSED`, and HT-09 reported a position inside it. Their logs will show that for this email. It's worth a line in the README.

## Where I'd change your assumptions

- **Assumption 3 ("order by seq") needs reset detection.** Track each truck's seq within one controller run. Treat a large drop in seq while the device clock moves forward as a restart, not as a duplicate.
- **Assumption 12 should cover implausible data, not just old data.** A position's confidence should depend on its age *and* whether its movement matches the reported speed. HT-09 looked fresh and was wrong. When in doubt, the possible area is the range the truck could have reached since its last believable position.
- **Finding 3 is right about acknowledgements but not about whether the command worked.** Replaying the same `command_id` tells you how the gateway acknowledged it. It can't rescue a command that was `ACCEPTED` and then ignored, which is Priya's complaint. That needs a check against telemetry with a deadline, then a retry under a *new* id, with the attempt count shown so the operator knows how many have been sent.
- **Assumption 13 (battery confidence "if time allows") should be in the MVP, kept simple:** drain rate compared with the rest of the fleet, and whether the truck can reach the bay on its current charge. HT-06 is a problem that needs action within the next minute, which meets your own alarm threshold. Sending it to the bay stays the operator's decision.
- **The blast rule needs a "hold before entry" half** (point 9). Your assumptions only cover getting trucks out.
- **Questions I'd add to your list:** Can the BAY itself be closed for a blast? `EXIT_ZONE` is rejected in the BAY, so remote driving would be the only way out. And is a reversing truck allowed to pass, or back into, a truck behind it?

## The riskiest part

**Blast enforcement when the data is bad.** It's a timed job (120 s, commands taking 1–6 s, a 20 s queue behind loading) running on data that can be frozen, reset, silent or garbled, with nobody watching. A bug there is the one result the brief won't forgive, and on a good day it won't show up. So I'd build the fake gateway with fault injection *before* the blast logic, and replay this capture's failures (frozen position, seq reset, silent truck) as tests.

The second risk is remote driving: the 500 ms deadman loop runs through the browser, the service and the reverse proxy on one OCPU.

## What I'd cut first, in order

1. **The plain-language question feature.** I'd drop it outright rather than defer it, because nothing in the brief asks for it.
2. **The built-but-off automatic resume after a blast.** Make it a one-click "resume all trucks the system held" instead.
3. **Gamepad support.** Keyboard only.
4. **A shift-handover view.**
5. **The per-lap battery model.** Fall back to drain rate compared with the fleet.

I wouldn't cut ingest validation, blast enforcement and its tests, checking that commands took effect, e-stop, reconnection, or the audit log.

Once you've disagreed or agreed on the points above, I'll write PLAN.md in one pass, about a page, using the four headings the brief asks for.

### Agent (2026-10-02T02:05:52.432Z)

The report script reproduces everything I found by hand in run 1, so the runs will be comparable. It also turned up two new facts about run 1:

- **HT-09 froze at exactly +180 s, the moment DECLINE went `CLOSED`.** That could be coincidence or how the sim works; run 2 should tell us which.
- **HT-09's battery drained at half the fleet rate** (0.64 against 1.27 %/min). Energy use tracks distance, so the battery agrees with the frozen position: the truck probably did stop, and the 3.0 m/s speed is what's wrong. That changes the problem from "position is stale" to "two signals disagree, and a third settles it". It's a better basis for a confidence model.

Run 2 finishes in about 12 minutes. Run 3 has to start at least 30 minutes after run 2 ends, otherwise it rejoins the same day, so it begins around 45 minutes from now.

Only two of the three runs have data so far. Run 3 never captured anything: it was stopped while still waiting to start. I restarted it a moment ago and it's receiving data, so I'll add its results in about 15 minutes.

## Runs 1 and 2

Both runs only listened; I sent no commands. Run 1 lasted 6 minutes and run 2 lasted 15.

### The link

| | Run 1 | Run 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Link drops | none | **45 s** at +374 s and **21 s** at +846 s |
| Heartbeat | every 2.0 s | same, apart from the drops |
| Truncated lines | 0.19% | 0.21% |
| Telemetry rate | ~5 Hz per truck | same |
| Duplicates | ~2% | ~2% |
| Arriving out of order | ~6–7% | ~6–7% |
| Missing | ~3% | ~3% |

- **The 45 s drop began one second after a `CLOSING` notice, using up 45 of the 120 s.** During the drop the gateway accepted the login and then closed the connection, as §1.1 says it will.
- **Reconnecting recovers the zone state.** The `hello` after reconnecting showed the zone as `CLOSING`, with its effective time.

### Blasts

| | Run 1 | Run 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | DECLINE (full cycle), L4_SOUTH (started at the end) | L4_SOUTH, DRAW_12, TIP (**cancelled**) |
| Notice | 120 s every time | 120 s every time |
| Closed for | 102 s | 103 s, 111 s |
| Spacing | about every 5 minutes | about every 5 minutes |

Nothing was enforcing the rule, so trucks drove into every closed zone. That's in their logs for this email.

### Truck faults

The same faults turn up each day; only the trucks change.

| Fault | Run 1 | Run 2 | What a straightforward client would get wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| Position frozen in a zone **as it closes**, while reporting 3 m/s | HT-09 | HT-07 | Data that looks fresh is wrong; the battery drain shows the truck stopped |
| Seq counter resets at about +100 s | HT-10 | HT-10 | Treats the new messages as duplicates and freezes the truck on screen |
| Weak pack, about 5× fleet drain | HT-06 (9.9% loaded, entering the incline) | HT-11 (**died, `BATTERY_DEPLETED`, in the incline**) | Trusts the gauge; the trucks only charge if below 25% at the bay |
| `HYD_PRESSURE_LOW` in the incline at about +330 s | HT-07 | HT-02 | This truck needs remote driving to get home |
| SoC sent as a fraction (0.6 for 60%) | HT-05 | HT-03 | Shows 0.6% |
| Malformed fields: null speed or SoC, string offset, lowercase state | HT-08 | HT-01 | Crashes, or shows nonsense |
| Clock about 58 minutes ahead | HT-11 | HT-04 | Works out ages from the device clock |
| Truck goes silent while the link is up (24–55 s gaps) | HT-03 | HT-08 | Treats silence as "nothing's changed" |

### Implications for the plan

1. **Freshness alone doesn't tell us a position is right.** Position confidence has to combine age, whether movement matches the reported speed, and whether the battery drain agrees.
2. **Blast enforcement has to cope with a link drop during the notice period.** The service has to act on the `hello` snapshot as soon as it reconnects, and the 120 s budget has to account for time lost to the drop.
3. **Problems are timed to land inside blast windows.** The frozen positions and the link drop each fell inside a blast window in at least one run. A zone with a frozen truck in it can't be honestly called clear.
4. **Battery prediction belongs in the MVP.** Run 2 shows what happens without it: the truck died in the incline.
5. **A cancelled blast needs handling.** Trucks we held for TIP need a one-click resume.

What we still haven't seen, because I sent no commands: accepted-but-ignored commands, `EXIT_ZONE` on a truck with a frozen position, how fast trucks reverse, commands queued behind loading, and leases. The probe run I suggested is the way to find those out, and it's still your call. When run 3 finishes I'll add its results and point out anything that breaks the pattern.

### Agent (2026-10-02T14:01:33.501Z)

Run 3 finished after the full 15 minutes. It confirms the fault list from runs 1 and 2, but disproves two patterns I'd suggested.

**Same as runs 1 and 2:**
- **Every fault type turned up again, on different trucks:**
  - SoC sent as a fraction: HT-12
  - Malformed fields: HT-02
  - Clock about 58 minutes ahead: HT-08
  - Seq reset: HT-01
  - Frozen position: HT-10
  - Truck going silent: HT-03
  - Weak pack: HT-06
  - `HYD_PRESSURE_LOW`: HT-11
- **The weak pack died in the incline again.** HT-06 went from 43.8% to 0, ending with `BATTERY_DEPLETED` at +508 s. That's two dead trucks out of two runs long enough to see it.
- **The link dropped for 45 s, 17 s after an L4_SOUTH `CLOSING`.** That's twice in two runs that a drop has eaten into a blast notice. A second drop started at +872 s and was still going when the capture ended.
- **A blast was cancelled again.** L4_SOUTH went `OPEN CANCELLED` 31 s after we reconnected.
- Notice was 120 s every time, and about 0.2% of lines were truncated.

**Different from what I'd said:**
- **Frozen positions aren't tied to closures.** HT-10 froze at 1600 m, the end of TIP, at +160 s, and TIP wasn't closing. So I'm withdrawing "problems are timed to land inside blast windows" for frozen positions; it holds only for the link drops. The battery still confirmed the truck had stopped (0.24 %/min against 1.27).
- **The seq reset isn't always HT-10 or always at about +100 s.** This time it was HT-01 at +178 s.
- **`HYD_PRESSURE_LOW` isn't always in the incline.** This time it hit in TIP.
- **Closures vary in length.** These lasted 74 s and 66 s; in runs 1 and 2 they lasted about 105 s.

**The conclusion stands:** each day uses the same set of faults, with the truck, place and time randomised. Three runs is a reasonable basis for the assumptions now. The main change since my earlier list is to drop the "closure-timed" claim and replace it with "link drops have landed inside two of the three runs' blast notices".

Sending probe commands is still the remaining unknown. Do you want that run before we settle the assumptions, or shall I go ahead and propose the revised assumptions, then write PLAN.md?

**What it sends:** nine steps, S1–S9, each listed in the dry-run output. All commands carry `operator_id: "probe"` and ids of the form `probe-<run>-<n>`, so they're easy to pick out in their statutory log. It takes about 10–15 minutes, mostly S2 waiting for a truck to start loading and S9 waiting for a frozen one.

**What to check before going live:**
- **S5 moves a truck by hand,** at throttle 0.3 for 3 s, roughly 3–4 m forward. Trucks can't sense collisions, and the probe doesn't check for a truck close ahead.
- **S6 e-stops a truck,** then clears the e-stop and resumes it.
- **S7 sends four malformed commands to HT-01.** They should all be rejected. If one is accepted anyway, cleanup resumes HT-01.
- **Cleanup always runs, including after Ctrl-C.** It releases any leases the probe holds, clears its e-stops and resumes every truck it touched.
- **No `RESUME` while the truck's zone, or the next zone ahead, isn't `OPEN`.** Those trucks are left held and listed at the end for you to resume by hand. I added this guard after the first draft, which would have resumed trucks into a closing zone under the `probe` name.
- **Steps only choose trucks in `OPEN` zones**, never in the bay or a zone that's `CLOSING`, and never a truck with faults or malformed data.

**Its limits:**
- Trucks are chosen from telemetry, which we know can be wrong. A frozen truck could be picked for S1 and look like a stopped command.
- If the link drops during a step, it replays any unacknowledged `command_id`s after reconnecting, which also tests finding 3. But steps that time out don't retry; they just record the timeout.

Say if you'd like any step dropped, S5 and S6 especially, before you run it.

### Agent (2026-10-02T14:18:28.770Z)

The probe ran all nine steps in about 5 minutes and cleanup finished. The raw log shows more than the probe's own printout did, partly because my S1 code miscounted acks for a resent id. Everything below comes from the raw capture.

## What the commands actually did

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| **S1 hold/resume** | **The `HOLD`'s ack was lost, but HT-01 stopped 3.2 s after the send anyway.** Resending the same `command_id` brought back `ACCEPTED` without running it twice, so recovering an outcome by replaying the id works. A different payload under the same id got `COMMAND_ID_REUSED`. A message arriving out of order briefly showed the truck `TRAMMING` again after it was `HOLDING`. |
| **S2 queued hold** | **Skipped.** DRAW_12 was under a blast for the first 3 minutes, so no truck was loading. We still don't know how commands queue behind loading. |
| **S3 `EXIT_ZONE`** | HT-05 was 145 m into DECLINE. **It reversed at 3.0 m/s, the full autonomous speed, back up the decline and stopped 2 m inside the bay.** That took 53 s. A reversing truck heads straight toward the trucks coming down behind it. |
| **S4 lease expiry** | Deadman engaged after 0.42 s. A `HOLD` sent while the lease was held came back `LEASE_HELD` with `holder: "probe"`. The lease `EXPIRED` after 10.1 s and the truck stayed `HOLDING`. |
| **S4, continued** | **The `RESUME` was `ACCEPTED`, and then HT-02 sat `HOLDING` for 70 s.** A second `RESUME` under a new id moved it within 1.3 s. This is Priya's complaint ("got the command, and then the truck just… doesn't"), seen live. Cleanup only noticed because it checked the truck's state. |
| **S5 drive** | At throttle 0.3 for 3 s, the truck moved 2.7 m. **Drive echoes came back 200–620 ms after sending**, so the worst case is longer than the 500 ms deadman. After `RELEASE_CONTROL` the truck went to `HOLDING`, as the spec says. |
| **S6 e-stop** | `ESTOPPED` within 0.3 s. A `HOLD` got `ESTOP_ACTIVE`. After `CLEAR_ESTOP` the truck was `HOLDING`. All as the spec says. |
| **S7 bad commands** | Every rejection matched §4.5. An unparseable line is acked with `vehicle_id: null`. |
| **S8 faulted truck** | `INTERLOCK_ACTIVE`, as expected. |
| **S9 frozen truck** | **HT-10's whole telemetry message was frozen.** Every field stayed identical for 5 minutes, including SoC at 42.52, and only `seq` counted up. **The gateway accepted `EXIT_ZONE`, but its later `RESUME` came back `INVALID_STATE`.** That means the real truck was neither holding nor idle, so it was doing something we couldn't see. We can't confirm a command took effect on a truck we can't observe. |

Two more findings from the probe session:
- **Two zones were `CLOSING` at the same time** (DRAW_12 and TIP) when the probe connected. Every earlier run had one blast at a time.
- **HT-10 may be left in an unknown state.** Its last command from us was rejected, so it may still be held near TIP. It doesn't matter much in the sim, which starts a fresh day after 30 idle minutes. I won't send it anything more unless you want me to.

## What changes for the plan

1. **`ACCEPTED` doesn't mean the command worked.** S4 showed it live: an accepted command was ignored. Every supervisory command has to be confirmed in telemetry within a deadline. If it isn't, retry under a new id, show the number of attempts, and alert if it still fails. This goes into the core of the command handling, not on the list of extras.
2. **Frozen telemetry repeats the whole message, so there's nothing to cross-check on that truck.** The battery check I suggested earlier can't catch this kind: the SoC freezes with everything else. The test is simpler: if seq keeps rising while every other field stays identical, the data is dead. Treat the truck as "position unknown, could be anywhere it could have reached", and never count it as clear.
3. **The probe confirmed reversing at 3.0 m/s.** So the time to clear a zone is the distance to the nearer edge divided by 3.0 (2.0 if loaded), plus up to 6 s for the command to act.
4. **Driving latency can exceed the deadman.** Echoes took up to 620 ms against a 500 ms deadman. The remote-driving view needs a visible measure of lag, which is Dave's "not knowing if it's lagging".
5. **More than one zone can close at once,** so the blast logic needs to handle several zones together.

## Where things are kept

The three captures, the probe log, `report.py` and `probe.py` are all in the session scratchpad. The scratchpad is deleted when this session ends. I've saved a short summary of these findings to my memory so the next session has them. The raw files would also make good test fixtures, and the brief wants the agent context kept in the repo. I'd suggest copying the scripts and a trimmed, email-free capture into something like `research/` in the repo. That needs your say-so, since the repo goes public.

I'm ready to propose the revised assumptions and write PLAN.md whenever you are.

40	**2. The protocol already encodes an autonomy policy: stopping is cheap,
41	starting is deliberate.** A truck can be stopped ten ways, four with no human
42	at all (deadman at 500 ms, lease idle expiry at 10 s, lease revocation, estop).
43	It can be started two ways, both a deliberate human act: `RESUME` — which is
44	*rejected* with `INVALID_STATE` unless the truck is already `HOLDING` or
45	`IDLE` — and fresh drive input after a deadman. §6.4 is decisive: when a lease
46	expires the vehicle holds and "does **not** return to autonomous operation by
47	itself." Match this. Our system stops trucks freely and never starts one by default 
48	without a person.
49	
50	**3. Reconnection is solvable, not lossy.** The gateway queues nothing for a
51	disconnected client, so an ack for an in-flight command is lost. But §5 says
52	resending the same `command_id` with the same payload returns the original
53	result without re-executing. So on reconnect, replay in-flight `command_id`s
54	and the gateway tells us what actually happened. Idempotent, no double
55	execution.
56	
57	**4. Automation precision is a function of data confidence.** When a position
58	is fresh, evacuate exactly the trucks in the zone — Lena: "don't stop trucks

60	**blunter**, not bolder: widen the set, hold more trucks, and tell the operator
61	we did and why. This inverts the usual instinct and the blast logic should be
62	built around it.

## Your four points, checked against the captures

1. **The device clock doesn't separate a frozen truck from a parked one.** It keeps ticking in step with real time on all four frozen trucks. Your worry about my test was right, though: a loading truck also sends identical messages for its full 20 s. What does separate them is motion that contradicts position: every frozen truck reported `TRAMMING` at 2–3 m/s with no change in position. A truck that freezes while already stopped can't be detected from telemetry alone. CONTEXT.md and the research README both say so.
2. **The deadman risk is smaller than the 620 ms suggested.** Our drive messages went out 100–106 ms apart, and the deadman never tripped in 29 telemetry samples. That's only about 4 s of driving, so the research README marks it as a small sample.
3. **Retrying under a new id is now stated as safe, with queuing as the exception.** Both are in assumption 15. Queue behaviour is marked unverified, to be tested in the fake gateway.
4. **The 2.0 m/s loaded reverse speed is marked as assumed**, in assumption 6 and the research README.

Evacuation as coordinated (hold upstream first, then reverse) is assumption 16. It also answers your question 3 in both CONTEXT.md and PLAN.md, with the probe as evidence.

## Where I departed from what you asked

- **AI_LOG.md has two entries, not one.** The second is mine: I claimed twice that the frozen truck's battery "confirmed" it had stopped. Your clock question exposed it, because the battery was frozen along with everything else.
- **I added a ninth fixture beyond your list:** the link drop during a blast notice. The plan depends on it.
- **`.env.example` went into the research commit**, with an empty `ANTHROPIC_KEY`. The scripts don't read it, because nothing uses it yet and reading an unused key would be odd. The Anthropic SDK looks for `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` by default, so you may want that name when the key goes in.

## Decisions in PLAN.md you should check

- **Stack:** TypeScript on Node 22, SQLite through the built-in `node:sqlite`, and port 8090. You haven't approved any of these yet.
- **No automatic resume after a blast, not even built and switched off.** This **contradicts CONTEXT.md assumption 2**, which says "built but off by default". I didn't edit your assumption to match. One of the two needs to change.
- **No plain-language queries in this version.** This fits CONTEXT's "beyond MVP", but you mentioned adding a key for them later.
- **PLAN.md is about 830 words.** That's a page if you're generous with the brief's "one page is plenty".

    ## How it's tested
Against how it will be judged: unattended on an unseen site, and driven by a novice. Time is injected, so blast scenarios run in milliseconds.
Pure logic is table-tested per fault class; the nine research/fixtures/ are replayed as regressions. Blast safety is property-tested over thousands of seeded random days from the fake gateway, which knows true
positions and so checks two invariants — never a truck in a CLOSED zone without an alarm in time, never "clear" when it isn't — and counts unnecessary holds. Process kills, browser drops, stuck keys and slow reads are tested on purpose. A live soak runs beside an independent invariant monitor, and one person who has never seen it does three timed tasks. Detail in TESTING.md.

Then write TESTING.md as the spec agent tasks point at — which cases each task must pass. Each layer answers one way we'll be judged:

1. Injectable time, first. Hard to retrofit.
2. Pure-logic unit tests, table-driven:
   - loop geometry: distance to nearest boundary with wrap, direction, time to clear (empty measured, loaded assumed), the set of places a frozen truck could have reached
   - ingest, one case per fault class: fractional SoC flagged not scaled, truncated lines dropped and counted, lowercase state, string offset, null fields
   - restart versus duplicate
   - frozen detection: frozen TRAMMING flagged; loading, holding and idle in the bay NOT flagged — the negatives matter as much
   - the command registry: ack before and after telemetry, lost ack, duplicate ack, COMMAND_ID_REUSED, LEASE_HELD with holder, deadlines that depend on state, retry under a new id, and a retry never displacing a different queued command
3. Fixture replay: each research/fixtures file through ingest and state, asserting what the operator would see.
4. Property-based blast safety — the headline. Thousands of seeded random days mixing faults. The fake gateway knows true positions, so it's the
   oracle. Invariants:
   - never silent: no truck in a CLOSED zone unless a can't-clear alarm went
     up early enough, with the reason. Some cases are unwinnable (a faulted
     truck); the invariant is "never violated silently"
   - never wrongly clear: never recommend clear while the truth has a truck inside. This is our evidence for README §6
   - unnecessary holds counted as a metric, not a pass/fail, so over-stopping shows up as a regression
5. A fault-injection matrix: faults (link drop, lost ack,
   accepted-then-ignored, frozen, silent, seq reset, truncation, clock skew, duplicates, reordering, two zones, fault in zone, cancelled blast) against moments (steady, during CLOSING, during manual driving, during
reconnect). Fill the three we saw live first: link drop during the notice, frozen truck in a closing zone, two zones at once.
6. Process resilience:
   - kill the service mid-CLOSING and restart: it acts on the hello snapshot within the time left
   - browser drops mid-drive: truck stops on the deadman, the service synthesizes nothing
   - several browsers open: none opens its own gateway connection (16 per site)
   - slow ingest: the gateway drops a client more than 4 MB behind; prove we keep up
7. Driving: deadman through the relay, lag display accuracy, forced takeover mid-drive by a supervisor, e-stop wins while someone else drives. And a key held when the window loses focus: the browser never sends keyup, so the throttle sticks. On blur and visibility change send zero and stop streaming, with a test.
8. Multi-operator and audit: the lease holder sees a blocked command; only supervisors force takeover; operator_id can't be spoofed from the browser; Marta's "who moved HT-06 at 3:12?" answered by a query, with rule and inputs for system actions; the log is append-only and survives a restart.
9. UI with Playwright — actually load the page. Live, old, silent and contradicted data look different. Site link down: the picture visibly ages and a banner says so. Service down: the browser says disconnected,
not a frozen picture shown as current. Two links, two tests.
10. Live soak: 15+ minutes unattended across fresh days, beside an independent invariant monitor — a passive observer computing "truck in a closed zone" from raw telemetry on its own. If the product and the monitor disagree, one is wrong.
11. Novice test: someone who's never seen it, three timed tasks — answer "is L4 South clear?" (target 10 s), drive a faulted truck to the bay, e-stop a truck. Their stumbles become the README walkthrough.
12. Scale: the fake gateway at 140 trucks × 5 Hz on one OCPU, to see what breaks first, so README §10 has a measurement, not a guess.
13. Packaging: fresh clone, docker compose up with only the three GATEWAY_* variables and no Anthropic key, on x86 and ARM, in CI.

## What I'd change in the test strategy

**1. "Never wrongly clear" checked against true positions will fail by design.** A truck that freezes while stopped and then moves can't be detected from telemetry, as we already noted. The fake gateway knows where it really is, so it will find violations no code can prevent.
- **Proposal:** test both rules against true positions for every fault we *can* detect.
- Run the undetectable fault separately. There, violations are counted and reported as the README §5 figure for "where it can't enforce", rather than hidden or left to fail the suite.
- CLAUDE.md states the product rule as "might be inside", meaning based on what the system can know. The test checks against the truth.

**2. "Alarm early enough" needs a number.** Ken has to be able to hold the shot. My suggestion: the can't-clear alarm must go up within 10 s of `CLOSING`, or within 10 s of the data first allowing that conclusion, whichever is later. Your call.

**3. The fake gateway's accuracy limits everything.** We built it from three runs and one probe. Queuing is unverified and the loaded reverse speed is assumed. If the fake is wrong, thousands of seeded days only prove our code agrees with our own misunderstanding.
- **Proposal:** add a conformance check. The fake must reproduce the fixtures' fault signatures and the probe's acks, and must sit close to the live captures' statistics.

**4. The live-soak monitor isn't independent of the data.** It reads the same telemetry, so it's fooled by the same frozen and silent trucks. If it disagrees with the product, one of them is wrong. If they agree, that doesn't prove either is right. I'd say exactly that in TESTING.md, and keep the monitor's code fully separate from the product's.

**5. Proportion: these are the cuts I'd make deliberately.**
- **Seeded days.** One 15-minute day is about 54,000 messages, so thousands of days is over 100 million. CI runs about 200 seeds; the full set runs before submission. Any seed that fails becomes a permanent regression test.
- **Scale (layer 12).** One benchmark run with the result written down, not a CI job.
- **Playwright.** Only what you listed: the four data states, the two link-down tests and the stuck key. No broad UI suite.
- **ARM CI.** GitHub's ARM runners are free for public repos. If the repo stays private until submission, the ARM build runs under emulation: slow, but enough to prove it builds and starts.
- **Novice test.** It needs a person, and that's you. I can prepare the script and the timer.

Everything else is in proportion. The fake gateway is the big cost, and it's on the critical path either way.

**One addition:** a check under layer 13 that the system comes back after a reboot. The box's current gap is exactly what that would catch.

## The deploy box

**I recommend installing Docker CE on dronehal1.** Docker's RHEL 9 repository has aarch64 builds that work on Oracle Linux 9. With `restart: unless-stopped` and `docker.service` enabled, it survives a reboot, and the box runs exactly what the graders run.
- **Cost:** about 100 MB of RAM for the Docker daemon, and slow image builds on one OCPU. Building multi-arch images in CI and pulling them avoids the slow builds.
- **Risk:** Docker rewrites firewall rules on a box already serving another project on 8080. Check that service immediately after installing.

**The alternative, systemd running the box's own Node**, avoids Docker but splits what we test from what we deploy. The box has Node 22, which prints the SQLite warning at every start. Podman, which ships with Oracle Linux 9, sits between the two, but I'm less sure `docker compose` behaves the same under it.

## Pending for step 4

When you've answered points 1–5, I'll commit PLAN.md with three changes:
- your "How it's tested" text, including any wording you change,
- alerting as an MVP item: "interrupt only for action needed in the next minute; everything else visible but silent, with the rule that silenced it inspectable",
- the stack line changed from Node 22 to Node 24.

Then TESTING.md.

Two things: the site has answered my four questions we previosuly sent, and I've reviewed TESTING.md. Do the answers first — they change some of the review.

## The answers

1. The operator and Ken talk directly, by radio. Ken calls about two minutes before firing, around when the system notice arrives, and doesn't fire until the operator says it's clear. If the operator isn't sure, they ask him to hold the shot — costly, but always right when in doubt. The gateway can't reach the blasting crew. Clearing people isn't our problem; clearing trucks is.
2. The system may restart trucks on its own once a zone reopens, whether the blast happened or was called off. No sign-off needed. The site wants trucks back at work without operators chasing each one.
3. Spacing is out of scope. Assume it's handled elsewhere; don't build for it. The simulator doesn't model trucks interacting — they never block or hit each other, even reversing.
4. The system acting on its own is expected, especially for blasts, since nights are one operator. Its actions go in the same log as the operators', showing what it did, when and why. That's a good answer for the inspector.

What that changes:

- Auto-resume is now MVP and on by default. When a zone reopens (CLEARED or CANCELLED), the system resumes the trucks IT held for that blast — never a truck an operator held, never one with a lease or a fault, and never into another zone that's closing or closed. The resume goes through command confirmation like any other command, and is logged as the system, with the rule and inputs.
- Coordinated evacuation is gone: drop upstream holds before reversing (assumption 16, L2.8, L3.7, and that half of PLAN's MVP item 3). With spacing out of scope they'd only be unnecessary stops. Hold-before-entry stays — that's about the zone, not spacing.
- A can't-clear alarm names the action: "radio the shot firer to hold the shot", with the truck, the zone and the reason.
- System and operator actions share one log, with what, when and why.

Don't edit PLAN.md's body. Record the four answers and what they changed in CONTEXT.md now (mark the questions answered; 5 and 6 stay open), and they'll go into PLAN's "What changed" section at the end. CLAUDE.md's "starting always does" needs to change to match answer 2.

## The TESTING.md review

Very well done! — the belief/truth split, the IDs and the task table are exactly right. Your four choices are fine, but the open thresholds need numbers early in the ingest task: L4.R1's 10 s rule means nothing until they're set. Two gaps I see:

1. A system that does nothing passes the blast suite. L4 rules on alarming (R1), on wrongly saying clear (R2a–c), and over-holding (M1). Nothing requires trucks to get out. A system that never moves a truck and alarms about every one passes R1, never says clear, and scores a perfect M1. CLAUDE.md invariant 5 reads as a permission ("may be inside only if an alarm went up"). Add L4.R0, against the truth: every truck that could have been cleared or held before entry is outside the zone when it closes — "could" meaning the data allowed it in time, the time to clear plus command delay fits in the time left, and it wasn't interlocked. The alarm is for the trucks that couldn't. Reword invariant 5 so the alarm never replaces evacuation.

2. Nothing says the site might be different. We'll be run against a site we haven't seen, but nowhere do the docs say to take the route, loop length, vehicle list and notice length from hello. Every number we have is from one site, and an agent will hardcode them. Add a CLAUDE.md invariant: nothing site-specific is a constant. Then a test where the fake gateway serves a different site — different route, truck count, shorter notice — and the whole L4 suite still passes.

Smaller:

- Auto-resume (from answer 2): every truck the system held for a zone is resumed within a bound after it reopens, unless still blocked; an operator's hold is never resumed; nothing is resumed into a closing or closed zone. Plus a metric: time trucks sat after a reopen.
- Operator commands that route through a closing zone: RETURN_TO_BAY takes "the shorter direction", which can pass through one; an operator RESUME of a truck held for a blast; and EXIT_ZONE picks the nearest boundary itself, which can land a truck in an adjacent zone that's also closing. The safety check sits below operator commands too — test all three.
- The three MVP items with no cases: alerting (which events interrupt, which are silent, the silencing rule visible); battery warnings (drain against the fleet, can it reach the bay); and hand-back after driving — release leaves the truck HOLDING, so the UI has to make the RESUME step obvious. <details><summary>Result</summary>

```
## Invariants

These are not negotiable. If a task seems to need one broken, stop and ask.

1. **Time is injected.** No component reads the wall clock directly. Everything takes a clock,
   so blast scenarios run in milliseconds in tests.
2. **`operator_id` comes from the server-side session,** never from the browser's payload.
3. **Drive input is relayed only while fresh,** and never re-sent or synthesised by the service.
   Silence means stop: a browser that goes quiet must let the deadman stop the truck.
4. **No model on the control path.** Nothing an LLM produces sends a command.
5. **Blast safety: get every truck out that can be got out; alarm for the rest.** Every truck
   that can be cleared from a closing zone, or held before entering it, in the time left is
   outside when it closes. For a truck that can't, a can't-clear alarm ("radio the shot firer
   to hold the shot", with the truck, the zone and the reason) goes up within 10 s of
   `CLOSING`, or of the data first allowing that conclusion, whichever is later. The alarm
   never replaces evacuation (`TESTING.md` L4).
6. **Blast safety: never wrongly clear.** The system never recommends "clear" while any truck
   might be inside. "Might" includes old, silent and contradicted data.
7. **Nothing site-specific is a constant.** We will be run against a site we haven't seen.
   Route, segments, zones, loop length and vehicle list come from `hello`; notice length comes
   from each `zone_event`'s `effective_at_ms`. Speeds and delays are parameters with their source
   noted (spec or measured), never literals scattered through the code.

The rest of `CONTEXT.md`'s assumptions bind too. The ones most often forgotten: `ACCEPTED` is
not done, so confirm the effect in telemetry. Order by `seq` within a controller run and age
against `server_time_ms`, never the device clock. Stopping needs no person. The system restarts
only trucks it held for a blast, once that zone reopens; every other hold waits for a person. The
safety check sits below every command path, operators' included.

## How to work
```

### Prompt (2026-10-02T20:21:21.076Z)

Agree: start with the foundation as laid out, then the fake gateway and ingest in parallel.

Your choices:
- Auto-resume within 15 s: yes.
- E-stop while the link is down: not automatic on reconnect. Stopping is safe in isolation, not in context — a stale e-stop revokes leases, so it could strand an operator limp-homing a faulted truck out of a closing zone. Keep it pending and visible with a cancel. Send it automatically only if the link returns within 10 s; after that, show the truck's current state and ask the operator to confirm again.
- Escalation: re-alert at 15 minutes, supervisor at 30. But on nights the operator is alone and is the supervisor, so escalation there means more persistent alerting to that same person, not handing it on.
- Note "ten fixtures, not nine" for PLAN's What changed.

The UI. Building it at step 6 is fine; designing it that late isn't. Operator experience is one of the five graded criteria, a novice will drive a truck through it, and the decision log needs an operator-experience decision. So alongside the foundation, write UI.md — the design spec the UI task will build from — and plan to prototype it against replayed fixtures, so it's designed around frozen, silent and stale trucks from the start. Direction:

- A track diagram, not a map: the loop drawn like a metro line from hello's route, zones as bands showing OPEN, a CLOSING countdown or CLOSED, trucks as chips on the line.
- Position as a range when we're unsure: a frozen or silent truck drawn as a bar over everywhere it could have reached, not a dot.
- A zone clearance panel: for each closing zone, CLEAR, NOT CLEAR or UNSURE, with the doubts listed and, when not clear, "Radio the shot firer to hold the shot." Priya's 10-second question should take 2.
- A fleet table sorted by attention: state, zone, SoC as the pack's number with a confidence flag, control mode with who holds the lease, the data state in words as well as colour, and the last command's outcome with its attempt count.
- Command outcomes as a timeline: sent, acknowledged, effect seen — or "retry 2 of 3", or failed with the reason in plain words.
- An attention tray: interrupts at the top, silent items below, each with the rule that silenced it; acknowledgements attributed.
- A driving view: lag meter (input age, echo age), deadman state, speed, distance to the next zone boundary and its status, and hand-back as an obvious two-step — Release, then Resume.
- E-stop in a fixed place on every view, distinct in shape as well as colour, with a visible "pending, not delivered" state.
- Two link indicators — site and service. When either drops, the picture visibly ages instead of freezing.
- Who else is on: operators logged in, and who holds which lease.
- Built for a 12-hour shift: dark, low glare, large type, calm by default — nothing moves or flashes unless it needs action. Sound only for interrupts, distinct tones, never continuous. Colour never carries meaning alone.
- An audit view that answers "who moved HT-06 at 3:12" directly.

Tell me if anything in that conflicts with the tests or the invariants before you write it. Keep UI.md to a page or two: principles, the screens, and the states each screen must show.

Commit order: foundation code with its tests (L1 first), then UI.md, then the fake gateway and ingest tasks. The queuing re-probe is approved once the foundation is in — ask me before it runs so I know when real commands go out.

  **Rules worth reviewing:**
  - **Restart vs reorder.** A lower seq is a new controller run only if the device clock moved forward *and* (the drop exceeds the window *or* the new seq is within the window). A late message from the old run, which has a higher seq but an older device time, is treated as old.
  - **Frozen.**
    - The clock starts at the first message reporting motion at an unchanged position, and at least one repeat is required.
    - The range is anchored at the last stationary report at that position, or else its first message.
    - Silence takes precedence: a frozen truck that goes quiet shows as silent, keeps its pre-freeze anchor, and its reason says its last data was frozen. The checker found this — I originally left it "contradicted" forever.
  - **Reachable range.**
    - Top speed is the mode's maximum, not the reported speed: 3.0 m/s auto, 4.0 m/s manual. The frozen HT-10 reported 2.0 loaded but had very probably dumped and left empty.
    - Silent, contradicted, manual, tasked or reversing trucks can be anywhere in both directions; other trucks only forward.
    - Range ends count as inside (closed), so a range touching a boundary is in both zones.
    - A truck with no valid position yet, or every truck before `hello`, could be anywhere on the loop.
  - **Fractional SoC.** A value of 1.0 or less is a fraction unless the pack drained smoothly into it, i.e. the previous reading was within 2 points. Exactly 0 is never flagged. It is never scaled, and battery conclusions are suppressed while it's flagged.
  - **Ages** are elapsed time on the injected clock since receipt. Timestamps are mapped onto server time through the learned offset. `t_device_ms` is used only for restart ordering and skew.
  - **Zones.** A route zone missing from `hello` has status `null` (unknown, never open). A `zone_event` older than what we already hold is dropped and counted.
  - **Battery warnings**, in order:
    - `DEPLETED` ("needs a tow").
    - `CANNOT_REACH_BAY`: not enough charge even by the shorter way.
    - `WONT_FINISH_LAP`: the forward duty cycle (load at the end of a `load` segment, dump at the end of a `dump` segment, from `hello`'s kinds) needs more than it has. The message says "return to bay now". It is skipped when the truck is about to charge or is already returning.

// Run the fake gateway over TLS on the real clock, for research/probe.py and by-hand checks.
//
//   openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1 -subj /CN=127.0.0.1 \
//     -addext subjectAltName=IP:127.0.0.1 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem
//   node fake/main.ts --key key.pem --cert cert.pem [--port 7443] [--seed 1] [--blasts random|none]
//                     [--fault <vehicle>:<code> ...]
//
// Then point a client at it with GATEWAY_HOST=127.0.0.1, GATEWAY_PORT and SSL_CERT_FILE=cert.pem.
// The default site is DLH-1 (fake/dlh1.ts). Never point a probe at the real gateway by accident:
// this prints the address it serves.
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { parseArgs } from 'node:util';
import { SystemClock } from '../src/clock.ts';
import { FakeGateway } from './gateway.ts';
import { DLH1 } from './dlh1.ts';
import { listenTls } from './tls.ts';

const { values } = parseArgs({
  options: {
    key: { type: 'string' },
    cert: { type: 'string' },
    host: { type: 'string', default: '127.0.0.1' },
    port: { type: 'string', default: '0' },
    seed: { type: 'string', default: '1' },
    blasts: { type: 'string', default: 'random' },
    fault: { type: 'string', multiple: true, default: [] },
  },
});
if (!values.key || !values.cert) {
  console.error('usage: node fake/main.ts --key key.pem --cert cert.pem [--port N] [--seed N] [--blasts random|none] [--fault VEHICLE:CODE]');
  process.exit(2);
}
if (values.blasts !== 'random' && values.blasts !== 'none') {
  console.error(`--blasts must be random or none, not ${values.blasts}`);
  process.exit(2);
}

const gw = new FakeGateway(new SystemClock(), { seed: Number(values.seed), site: DLH1, blasts: values.blasts });
for (const f of values.fault) {
  const [vehicle, code] = f.split(':');
  if (!vehicle || !code) { console.error(`--fault wants VEHICLE:CODE, not ${f}`); process.exit(2); }
  gw.injectFault(vehicle, code);
}
gw.start();
const server = await listenTls(gw, { key: readFileSync(values.key), cert: readFileSync(values.cert), host: values.host, port: Number(values.port) });
console.log(`fake gateway (site ${DLH1.site_id}, seed ${values.seed}) listening on ${values.host}:${server.port}`);

const shutdown = () => { gw.stop(); void server.close().then(() => process.exit(0)); };
process.on('SIGINT', shutdown);
process.on('SIGTERM', shutdown);

## The blast rules draft: `BLAST.md`, uncommitted, for your edit

It defines rules B1–B15, each with an id that the audit log records against system actions. The decisions most worth your attention:

- **B1: an unsure truck is held, never sent out.** `EXIT_ZONE` leaves whatever zone the truck is *actually* in, so a frozen truck that's really just outside could be driven *into* the closing zone.
- **B2: a confident truck that will leave on its own in time gets no command.**
- **B4: never send a truck into another zone that isn't open;** hold it and alarm instead.
- **B6: hold before entry, timed for when it's needed,** not at `CLOSING`.
- **B6a, new from the re-probe:** the end of the draw point is L4_SOUTH's boundary. I propose the system take the truck with `TAKE_CONTROL` there. It's immediate, and the truck then ends up `HOLDING`.
- **B7: never rely on cancelling a sent command.**
- **B11:** the CLEAR / NOT CLEAR / UNSURE rule.
- **B12:** auto-resume.

Six open points at the end need your decision. The biggest is **B6a**: it would be the one place the system takes manual control of a truck. I lean towards it, but it interrupts loading and shows "system" as a lease holder to operators.

// A recorder for the fake gateway that writes what research/capture.py writes for the live one:
// {kind, rx_ms, m | raw}, with 'connected', 'msg', 'unparseable' and 'closed_by_peer', and the same
// reconnect backoff (2, 4, 8, then 10 s). So research/report.py and test/helpers/radio-stats.ts can
// read a fake day exactly as they read a live capture (TESTING.md L0.C1, L0.C3).
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import type { Clock } from '../../src/clock.ts';
import type { FakeGateway } from '../../fake/gateway.ts';
import type { FixtureRecord } from './fixtures.ts';

export interface Capture {
  rows: FixtureRecord[];
  send(msg: object): void; // a command or drive message, recorded as 'sent' (as probe.py does)
  write(path: string): void;
}

export function capture(gw: FakeGateway, clock: Clock, email = '<redacted-email>'): Capture {
  const rows: FixtureRecord[] = [];
  let attempt = 0;
  let conn: ReturnType<FakeGateway['attach']> | null = null;
  const connect = () => {
    attempt++;
    let open = true;
    const c = gw.attach({
      write(line) {
        let m: unknown;
        try { m = JSON.parse(line); } catch { rows.push({ kind: 'unparseable', raw: line.slice(0, 500), rx_ms: clock.now() }); return; }
        rows.push({ kind: 'msg', m: m as Record<string, unknown>, rx_ms: clock.now() });
      },
      close() {
        if (!open) return;
        open = false;
        conn = null;
        rows.push({ kind: 'closed_by_peer', rx_ms: clock.now() });
        clock.setTimeout(connect, Math.min(2 ** Math.min(attempt, 4), 10) * 1000);
      },
    });
    conn = c;
    rows.push({ kind: 'connected', attempt, rx_ms: clock.now() });
    c.receive(JSON.stringify({ type: 'auth', email }));
  };
  connect();
  return {
    rows,
    send(msg) {
      const raw = JSON.stringify(msg);
      rows.push({ kind: 'sent', raw, rx_ms: clock.now() });
      conn?.receive(raw);
    },
    write(path) {
      writeFileSync(path, rows.map((r) => JSON.stringify({ ...r })).join('\n') + '\n');
    },
  };
}
```

  ## Security choices
  - **Passwords:** scrypt from `node:crypto`, at one of OWASP's minimum settings (about 280 ms per login on this Mac). The users file refuses a plain password field.
  - **User names:** an unknown name costs the same work as a wrong password, so timing doesn't reveal which names exist. Names starting with `system` are refused, because that is how the system's own commands are logged at the gateway.
  - **Sessions:**
    - A random 256-bit id in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie, held in memory, so a restart logs everyone out.
    - Every login gets a fresh id. The cookie is marked Secure only when the address it was reached at is https.
    - A session ends at logout, after 30 min with no request and no screen open, or at 14 h regardless.
    - An open screen keeps the session alive, because logging out a watched control-room screen would hide alarms.
    - Logout or expiry is audited and closes that session's screens immediately.
  - **Login throttling:** 5 failures in 15 min, counted per address and per address-plus-name, never per name alone. Someone mistyping Dave's password elsewhere can't lock Dave out.
  - **Audit and logs:**
    - Logins, logouts and failed logins go in the audit log. A failed login records the typed name only if it is a real user, because people type passwords into name fields.
    - The log never contains the email, a password or a session id. A test checks this.
  - **Every route needs a session** (L8.6), except the login page and its stylesheet.
  - **Requests from other sites:** the Host header must be one of the service's own addresses, which blocks DNS rebinding. The Origin must also be one of ours, and is required on every POST and on the WebSocket upgrade.
  - **Browser hardening:** a content security policy allowing scripts from this origin only, framing denied, nosniff, no-store. The referrer policy is `same-origin`: with `no-referrer`, Chrome sends `Origin: null` on the login form and every real login was refused. The browser test found that.
  - **WebSocket limits:**
    - 4 KB per message, binary refused.
    - 10 messages a second per browser, then disconnected if it keeps on.
    - At most 8 screens per login.
    - A browser that falls behind skips frames rather than getting a backlog.
    - ws errors are caught, so an oversized frame closes that one connection, not the process.
  - **The rest:**
    - Cancelling a pending e-stop is limited to whoever pressed it or a supervisor.
    - It listens on 127.0.0.1 by default.
    - The data directory is created owner-only.
    - The database, data directory, keys and certificates are gitignored.
    - Blast safety still uses the allow-all gate. That is logged at start-up as "BLAST SAFETY NOT ACTIVE" and shown in a banner on every screen.
  
  ## Before a real mine used it
  - Single sign-on and short-lived contractor accounts in place of a users file.
  - Sessions that survive a restart, with server-side revocation.
  - TLS end to end, with the cookie always Secure.
  - A limit on how many logins can be checking passwords at once, since an attacker with many addresses can still burn CPU on scrypt.
  - Re-authentication for supervisor actions such as forced takeover, and per-action permissions.

Node 24.15 or later. From a fresh clone:

npm ci

state, the command log and the HTTP server; any number of browsers connect to it.

| `PORT` | no | `8090` | 8080 is taken on the deploy box |
| `HOST` | no | `127.0.0.1` | the address to listen on; put a TLS proxy in front for anything else |

| `DATA_DIR` | no | `data` | where the SQLite command and audit log is kept |
| `USERS_FILE` | no | `config/users.demo.json` | the operators; see below |

## The deploy

- **Docker CE 29.8 is installed,** with `docker.service` enabled at boot and the container set to `restart: unless-stopped`. Docker added a firewall zone for its own bridge only; the public zone still allows just http, https and ssh.
- **Docker publishes on `127.0.0.1:8090` only.** I added a Dockerfile and `compose.yaml` to the repo: the image runs as an unprivileged user and keeps its database in a volume.
- **L13.3 is verified on the exact arm64 image:** Node 24.15.0, `node:sqlite`, no warning.
- **The new Caddy block** is `dlh.150-136-98-129.sslip.io` → `127.0.0.1:8090`. The existing site block is untouched. I validated the new file as a copy, as the `caddy` user, before installing it, backed up the original as `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile.bak-20261004-012149`, and reloaded. Caddy's PID didn't change, so it was a reload, not a restart. Let's Encrypt issued the certificate.
- **The public address is configured** with `PUBLIC_ORIGIN`. Through the proxy, login works, the session cookie is `Secure`, a cross-origin login gets 403, and a WebSocket without a session gets 401.
- **The other site was unchanged every time I checked:** 401 through Caddy and 200 direct, at baseline, after the Docker install, after the Caddy reload, and after the redeploy.

**What the deploy caught (AI_LOG entry 6):** every login was logged as coming from Docker's bridge address. Login throttling counts per address, so five wrong passwords from anyone would have locked every operator out for 15 minutes. `TRUST_PROXY` now takes the real address from Caddy's forwarded header; compose sets it, which is safe only because the port is published on localhost. I redeployed and checked in the production log that logins now carry the real address.

**My own slip:** the alarm type I committed yesterday had a zone name in a comment, which broke L1.3 on main. I'd run only the type-checker, not the tests. The truck-detail agent caught it, and I applied its fix to main unchanged.

3. **Not done:** the reboot check (L13.5) needs a reboot of a box another project uses, so it's your call and your window. The amd64 build (L13.2) is untested, since there's no Docker on this Mac; CI can cover it.

1. Reads the current project code to understand the app.

single-provider.

Tone can be a preset (`default`, `polished`, `yc-parody`, `chaotic`, `deadpan`, `cinematic`, `app-store`) or a creative direction such as "fake Series A launch from 2016", "museum exhibit", or "overproduced mobile game ad".

When the user gives freeform tone direction, map it to the nearest preset for pacing and structure, but preserve the user's direction in the plan and composition brief.

## Narration guidance

## Tone system

Seven tone presets ship with `/brag`. Each changes scripting energy, pacing, typography personality, and transition style. Presets are defaults, not limits.

Full definitions: [references/tones.md](references/tones.md)

| Tone | Energy | One-liner |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | Playful, clean, postable | The good-vibes default |
| `polished` | Serious, elegant | For projects that are not jokes |
| `yc-parody` | Deadpan startup energy | Fake seriousness applied to absurd projects |
| `chaotic` | Fast, loud, aggressive | Over-the-top and unhinged |
| `deadpan` | Calm, dry, understated | The joke is that nothing is a joke |
| `cinematic` | Dramatic, trailer-scale | Big motion, bigger claims |
| `app-store` | Smooth, feature-card clean | Corporate but not boring |

Always allow a freeform creative direction to refine or override the preset.

---

## Creative laws

These apply to every brag video regardless of tone.

**Short.** 15–25 seconds. Not one second more without a reason.

**Readable.** Keep the pace high through motion and cuts, never by flashing text. Every line a viewer must read holds long enough to read it (short label ~0.8s settled; a sentence ~0.3s per word). Fast-in, then hold — never fast-in, then gone.

**Specific.** The video must feel like it was made for this exact project, not any project.

**Show the thing.** At least one scene must display actual UI, copy, or a key visual from the product. No abstract filler.

**No generic SaaS language.** "Streamline your workflow" is banned. Use the project's actual copy and claims.

**The hook is everything.** The first 2 seconds determine whether someone keeps watching. Plan the hook before anything else.

**Funny earns its place.** Humor should come from the project's absurdity, not from trying to be funny.

**Pattern:**
```
Hook (2-3s) → Reveal (2-4s) → 2-3 sharp highlights (5-12s) → Punchline/outro (2-4s)
```

Adapt this. Not every project needs exactly 3 highlights. The pattern is a starting shape, not a template.

  - **`src/ui/overview.ts`:** the clearance panel goes UNSURE while the site link is down, keeps the last call made with the link up, and the fleet table gets a restart marker for about a minute.
  - **`src/live.ts`:** the hub runs alerting on every tick, with or without a screen open. New browser messages:
    - `ack` takes the operator from the session; interrupts and acknowledgements go in the SQLite audit log.
    - `watch` sends one screen its truck's timeline.
    - `history` answers the audit query from `store.history()`.
    - It also tracks who left each holding truck there.
  - **`src/ui/app.ts`, `index.html`, `overview.css`:**
    - The tray: interrupts on top, then notices for you, then a collapsible silent list.
    - Sound: one short tone pattern per alert, a different one for blast, link and command problems. While unarmed it reads "Sound off: N alarms not heard".
    - The detail drawer opens from the table, the track or `#truck=ID`; the audit drawer opens from the header.
    - Clearance is never greyed. If the browser loses the service, every row turns UNSURE with the age of the last call.
  - **`PARAMS`:** added `persistentAlertEvery`, `noticeItemFor`, `restartMarkerFor` and `auditWindowDefault`, each with its source.
  - **Test helpers:** `FakeSite` now accepts blast specs and truck placements.
  - **Breaking change:** `LiveState.alarms` is replaced by `attention`, `clearance`, `held` and `restarts`. `test/live.test.ts`, `test/live.browser.ts` and `test/ui.browser.ts` are updated; the two browser tests now check that the track is greyed rather than the whole of `main`.
  
  ### Design choices UI.md didn't decide
  1. **What "logged in" means for escalation:** a person with a screen open.
  2. **Escalation with nobody to hand it to.** With a supervisor and others on, it goes to the supervisor, then reminds them every 15 min. With only the supervisor on (nights), it alerts them every 60 s. With no supervisor on, it alerts every screen every 60 s and says "phone the supervisor".
  3. **An interrupt resolved before anyone acknowledged it** stays in the tray, marked resolved, silent, until someone acknowledges it.
  4. **One cause, one alarm:** a silent alarm raised again as an interrupt is upgraded and alerts once; an open alarm is never quietly downgraded.
  5. **Battery:** both "cannot reach the bay" and "won't finish its lap" interrupt, because each says "return to bay now". A depleted truck is silent; it needs a tow.
  6. **Failed commands** interrupt only on a truck in, possibly in, or next to enter a closing zone, or for any e-stop. Otherwise they are silent. A failed-command alarm ends when acknowledged or when a later command on that truck is confirmed.
  7. **During a site-link outage** there is one link item and no per-truck "old" or "silent" items. Old data is otherwise a silent item, so the silent list changes often.
  8. **Items with nothing that ends them** (controller restart, a lost ack later confirmed) leave the tray after 10 min; truck detail keeps them.
  9. **Only interrupts and their acknowledgements are written to the SQLite audit log**, not silent items.
  10. **Buttons stay pressable** and the site or safety check refuses with the reason. Only what can never work is disabled: Take control on a depleted truck, or while someone else drives. A supervisor additionally gets "Take over from X".
  11. **"Can't verify"** is worked out in the UI: an open command, or one failed for no effect, on a truck whose data is silent or frozen.
  12. **"Held by"** comes from the latest confirmed Hold, Release, Exit zone or Clear e-stop command, or the latest lease event. If unknown it says so.
  13. **The audit view** defaults to ±10 min (2 min to 6 h selectable), uses the browser's local time, and lists commands only.
  14. **One tone pattern per frame at most**, the most urgent first.
  15. **Take control with no driving view yet:** the detail says "You have control. Driving from the browser is not in this build. Release…".
  
  ### What I need from the blast engine
  - **Alarms in the shared shape.** It should raise its can't-clear alarms as events in the `src/alarms.ts` shape. The service wires them in with `hub.attention.apply(event)` and passes `provisionalBlast: () => false` to the hub. Keys should be one per truck and zone, `interrupt: true`, `action` "Radio the shot firer to hold the shot", and `rule` the rule id with words. It should clear them per its B9 rule.
  - **Its own verdict for the panel.** It should supply a function matching the `VerdictFn` type in `src/ui/overview.ts`, passed to the hub as `verdict`. The hub already keeps the last call and turns every row UNSURE while the link is down (B13).
  - **A real "can't verify" status (B16).** Ideally from the registry, rather than my UI-side inference.
  - **Hold reasons.** Its holds and their reasons, so "held by system:B6" shows the rule; today it would come from its confirmed HOLD records.
  - **The safety gate.** When it replaces `ALLOW_ALL_GATE_NO_BLAST_SAFETY`, its refusal text is shown as is in the detail's result line and timeline, so it should say why and what would allow it.
  
  ### Known limits
  - Alarm store, truck notes and held-by live in memory and start again if the service restarts; the SQLite audit rows remain.
  - The audit view assumes the browser's clock is close to server time.

  - **R3 (real failure):** pessimistic, live day, seed 1. HT-06 was resumed 19.9 s after TIP reopened. Its first two B12 RESUMEs were both accepted and then ignored by the fake (the truth log confirms it). With an 8 s confirmation deadline, R3's 15 s budget can't absorb that.
  - **Earlier failures, now fixed:** R3 failures on spec seeds 1, 2 and 3 were an engine bug. A HOLD to a frozen truck stays "can't verify" all day and blocked both the resume and the next blast's HOLD. Fixed in `d9ba554`, with a test I checked fails without the fix.
  - **Metrics on those few days:**
    - M1: about 3–4 unnecessary holds per day out of about 9.
    - M2: median about 3–5 s, worst about 50 s.
    - M3: about 4 false alarms per day out of 5. Most are B1 alarms for silent or frozen trucks whose range touches the zone, which is what B1 and B11 say to do.
  
  ### Commits, in order
  1. `d15a614` Path prediction and its parameters (L2.7, L2.56, L2.57).
  2. `80d191c` Registry, its own commit: commands to a silent or frozen truck end "can't verify", not failed (B16).
  3. `0159419` Clearance: the engine's verdict; link down makes every zone not open UNSURE (B11, B13). This includes one line in `src/ui/overview.ts`.
  4. `1c3cdcc` The engine, `src/blast.ts` (B1–B15), its scenario tests, and the `engine_state` table in the store (B14).
  5. `881c960` The engine runs in the service; the live frame carries `clearance` (with `lastWhileUp`) and `blastAlarms`.
  6. `d3c38b5` **The gate swap.**
  7. `4278cd1` Gate tests (L2.50–L2.54); the test rig now uses the real gate.
  8. `d9ba554` Engine fix (the unverified HOLD), plus fewer evaluations: a day went from about 17 s to about 5 s.
  9. `7771d0c` The L4 harness, `tools/l4.ts`, `test/l4.slow.ts`, `npm run test:l4`, and `tools` added to tsconfig.
  10. `b7c4101` The live frame also carries `blastHolds`.
  
  ### Where BLAST.md was ambiguous or seemed wrong, and what I did
  - **B2's last safe moment:** I implemented it literally. It is the latest moment an EXIT_ZONE sent then, acting after the full 6 s delay from where the truck will be, still gets it out. So a truck about to leave on its own can still get an EXIT_ZONE at that moment. This adds to M1.
  - **B4, "that it cannot also clear":** EXIT_ZONE stops 2 m outside and holds, so it can never clear the next zone too. If the landing zone is not open, the engine holds and alarms.
  - **B8:** an EXIT_ZONE that B4 has allowed beats a B6 hold for another zone, because it stops in an open zone. TAKE_CONTROL beats everything.
  - **B10:** a truck driving out of the bay on its own in time gets no alarm. Every other truck in the bay is alarmed at once.
  - **B1, "before it reopens":** the reopen time is never given. The engine holds when the truck's range overlaps the zone, or is within the hold lead of it.
  - **B12:**
    - The engine resumes only trucks that were working (tramming, loading, dumping or charging) when it first held them.
    - The gate refuses to resume a silent or frozen truck while any zone is not open. The L4 oracle counts these as R3 exclusions, with the reason given.
    - The frozen truck therefore stays held until every zone is open.
  - **B6a:**
    - A charging truck is taken at once, because the charge rate is guessed.
    - A loading or dumping truck is taken 8 s before its work is due to end.
    - The lease is left to expire on its own; the engine never releases it.
  - **Planning speed:** the engine plans a loaded reverse at 1.5 m/s (the pessimistic figure) for alarms and last safe moments.
  - **B13:** with the link down, UNSURE overrides NOT CLEAR.
  - **No B1 HOLD mid-exit:** B1 does not HOLD a truck the engine is already getting out with EXIT_ZONE.
  - **L1.2:** the time is measured from CLOSING to the resume, after a warm-up run. A cold first run takes about 170–250 ms. It passes this way; it does not pass if setup and teardown are included.
  - **The oracle's own choices** are written beside the code in `test/helpers/l4.ts`:
    - when the data allows a conclusion
    - a 6 s worst command delay
    - R3 is timed from the reconnect if the link was down at the reopen
    - silent or frozen trucks are excluded from R0
  
  ### What the UI must show that it doesn't yet
  - `live.clearance[].lastWhileUp`, for "was CLEAR, 12 s ago".
  - `live.blastAlarms`, in the src/alarms.ts shape (interrupting, keyed, with an action), in the attention tray. The hub also still pushes them into the old `alarms` list.
  - `live.blastHolds`: "held for the blast in X; the system resumes it".
  - The new command status `unverified`: "can't verify: data silent/frozen".
  - The gate's refusal reasons.
  - Engine notes such as "EXIT_ZONE at its last safe moment in N s" and "taking control before loading ends". These are available from `engine.plan(v)` but are not in the frame yet.
  - Trucks under a system lease from B6a, shown as `system:B6a`.
  
  ### For the truck-detail merge
  - The pure verdict is `zoneClearance(zone, trucks, {linkUp})` in `src/clearance.ts`.
  - `engine.clearances(snapshot)` gives the per-zone view.
  - `engine.subscribe` emits src/alarms.ts `raise` and `clear` events, plus `notify` events for lease holders.
  - A `VerdictFn` adapter should be a one-liner over `zoneClearance`. I did not build against that branch.

The blast engine is built, but its 200-seed numbers aren't ready, so nothing has merged. The run is about 100 of 1,200 days in. With the driving agent loading the machine too, it needs roughly another 1.5 hours. I'll bring you the full tables when it finishes.

## The gate swap, ready for you to read

Commit `d3c38b5` on `task/05-blast-engine`, viewable with `git show d3c38b5`. It touches 4 files:
- **`src/gate.ts`** (new, 117 lines): the safety gate. Stopping is never refused. It refuses:
  - **`RESUME`** while the engine holds the truck for a zone that isn't open, or when resuming would carry the truck into such a zone before a hold could act;
  - **`RETURN_TO_BAY`** when the shorter way passes through a zone that isn't open;
  - **`EXIT_ZONE`** in the bay, to a truck whose position can't be trusted while a zone is closing, or when its nearest way out leads into a zone that isn't open.
- **`src/service.ts`:** installs the gate in place of the allow-all one, and drops the "blast safety not active" warning and banner.
- **Two test assertions** that checked for that warning now check that it's gone. That goes slightly beyond "only the gate swap", but without it the commit would fail its own tests. The agent flagged it for you.

## Early results: 3 seeds per version, 18 days, not the 200

- **R0, R2a, R2b, R4, R5:** no failures.
- **R3 (auto-resume within 15 s) fails once,** in the pessimistic version. Two `RESUME`s in a row were accepted and then ignored, and the fake's truth log confirms it. With an 8 s confirmation deadline per attempt, the truck resumed after 19.9 s. **This needs your call:** keep R3 at 15 s and report it as a measured limit under double failures, shorten the confirmation deadline for `RESUME` specifically, or loosen R3. I'd keep the rule and shorten the `RESUME` deadline. The cost here is production, a truck sitting 5 s too long, not safety.
- **An engine bug the runs caught, now fixed:** a `HOLD` sent to a frozen truck stayed "can't verify" all day, which blocked that truck's resume and its next blast hold. The agent added a test and checked it fails without the fix.
- **Metrics, on those 18 days only:**
  - **M1 (unnecessary holds):** 3–4 of about 9 per day.
  - **M2 (time sat after a reopen):** median 3–5 s, worst about 50 s.
  - **M3 (false alarms):** about 4 of every 5 can't-clear alarms.

**M3 is the number I'd watch.** Most of those are B1 alarms: a silent or frozen truck whose possible range touches the zone. That's exactly what B1 and B11 tell the engine to do, but an operator who sees four false alarms in five learns to ignore them, which is how Dave's old system got muted. One option is a different, quieter alarm for "can't confirm where this truck is" than for "a truck is in there and can't get out". I'll decide nothing until we have the 200-seed numbers.

## The agent's other choices

- **B2's last safe moment is implemented literally,** so a truck about to leave on its own can still be sent `EXIT_ZONE` at that moment. That adds to M1.
- **Alarms and last safe moments are planned with a loaded reverse speed of 1.5 m/s**, the pessimistic figure rather than the measured 2.0.
- **A silent or frozen truck isn't resumed** while any zone is closing or closed.
- **B6a takes a loading or dumping truck 8 s before its work is due to end,** and a charging truck at once, since the charge rate is only a guess.

## Before merge, beyond your review

The agent didn't rerun the full suites after its changes, because of the machine load; it ran only the affected test files. I'll run all four suites myself once the L4 run finishes and the machine is quieter.
